items.title: Determinants of Trust and Interaction with Voice Assistants in Sustainable Purchasing Behaviors
items.abstract: The increasing adoption of artificial intelligence-powered voice assistants presents new opportunities to understand their relationship with organic product purchasing behavior. In this context, this study aims to examine the relationship between perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use on engagement with voice assistants, considering the mediating role of trust and its relationship with purchasing behavior for organic products. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed using a non-probability sample of 473 university students in Ecuador. Data were analyzed using partial least-squares structural equation modeling. The findings revealed that perceived usefulness and ease of use were significantly associated with trust, but neither exhibited a significant direct relationship with engagement with voice assistants. However, trust significantly mediated both relationships, with perceived usefulness demonstrating a stronger indirect effect than perceived ease of use. Furthermore, trust was significantly associated with engagement with voice assistants, which in turn was positively associated with purchasing behavior for organic products. The study concludes that trust serves as a central psychological mechanism linking technology-related perceptions to engagement with voice assistants, providing empirical support for integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and Stimulus-Organism-Response framework in the context of sustainable consumption.

items.title: Developing an LLM-based documentation support system with care workers: a Research through Design study
items.abstract: Introduction Developing technologies that are both meaningful to stakeholders and wanted in care settings remains challenging, as such systems must align with existing care practices, stakeholder needs, and organizational realities. This paper presents the design and development of a prototypical large language model (LLM)-based documentation support system for long-term care that generates documentation from audio recordings of care worker–resident interactions. Methods Adopting a Research through Design approach, we involved stakeholders throughout a 15-month design process to iteratively shape the problem framing, the resulting system, and our understanding of the sociotechnical tensions surrounding its use. Across four study phases conducted in Austrian residential nursing homes, 43 unique care stakeholders (24 care workers and 19 residents) participated. Four mock care interactions were recorded for feasibility testing, followed by 40 recordings of real care interactions. Results All generated summaries contained information useful for care documentation, but also included inaccurate or documentation-irrelevant content. However, exposing the prototype to real-world practice revealed requirements that had not emerged during earlier design stages, highlighting the importance of value sensitive design considerations such as privacy and autonomy. Discussion We further identify challenges specific to LLM-based systems, including incorrect inferences. Beyond technical concerns, introducing the system revealed tensions affecting interactions between care workers and residents, as well as broader organizational and research-related dynamics. These findings contribute design knowledge for the development of LLM-based technologies in long-term care and demonstrate the value of sustained stakeholder involvement throughout the design process in surfacing sociotechnical requirements and tensions.

items.title: Developing and validating the AI-REFINE process to support pre-service science teachers in co-designing STEM lesson plans with generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI offers considerable potential for science lesson planning but poses risks of passive use and scientific hallucinations for pre-service science teachers (PSTs), indicating a need for structured co-design frameworks in science teacher education. This study aimed to develop and content-validate the AI-REFINE process, a six-step framework (Request & Articulate, Evaluate, Formulate, Iterate, Normalize, Export) for guiding PSTs in co-designing science-integrated STEM lesson plans with generative AI. The study comprised two phases. In Phase 1, a two-round Delphi study with nine science education experts was conducted to establish the content validity of the process; the Scale Content Validity Index (S-CVI/Ave) reached 0.97. In Phase 2, a six-week pilot study using a one-group pre-test/post-test design was conducted with 28 third-year natural science PSTs at a teacher education university in Vietnam. Co-design competency was assessed through two parallel lesson plan design tasks evaluated with an analytic rubric by two independent raters. Results showed a statistically significant increase in competency scores from pre-test (M = 5.77, SD = 1.07) to post-test (M = 7.80, SD = 1.18), t(27) = − 18.48, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d av = 1.80, a result corroborated by a non-parametric sensitivity analysis. Because the design did not include a control group, causal claims cannot be made; the findings showed preliminary promise for supporting PSTs’ co-design competency rather than establishing effectiveness. The study suggests that AI-REFINE is a content-valid framework with potential for guiding PSTs toward active human-in-the-loop co-design, and controlled experimental studies are recommended to examine its efficacy.

items.title: Development and Initial Validation of a Survey Instrument on Students’ Acceptance of and Motivation Toward Generative AI in Higher Education
items.abstract: Questionnaires on students’ acceptance of generative AI (GenAI) are multiplying, but few combine technology acceptance with the expectancy-value beliefs and psychological needs that shape learning, and few test whether scores predict what students actually do. This study reports the development and initial validation of the 45-item Values, Expectancy and Motivation Perception of AI in Education (VEM-AIEd) questionnaire, which has 15 three-item scales drawn from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, expectancy-value theory and self-determination theory, together with a scale on ethical considerations. Eighteen items, covering six scales, were negatively worded. Sport science students at a private higher education institution in Singapore (N = 140) completed the questionnaire in 2024. The designed 15-factor model fitted moderately (CFI= 0.868, RMSEA= 0.062, SRMR= 0.071) and far better than one- and two-factor alternatives. Thirteen scales showed good internal consistency (α = 0.78–0.87) and convergent validity (AVE ≥ 0.50); social influence and cost did not. Item wording, however, shaped the structure. Exploratory factor analysis separated negatively from positively worded items, and latent correlations averaged 0.53 among negatively worded scales but only 0.11 between negatively and positively worded scales, even where content overlapped (performance expectancy and utility value, r = 0.03). Six-week test–retest reliability was poor to moderate (ICC = 0.20–0.55), and no scale predicted students’ logged use of a course chatbot. A shorter, consistently worded version with seven scales and 21 items fitted well (CFI = 0.939) but requires confirmation in new samples. The findings caution against mixing item directions in GenAI acceptance instruments.

items.title: Digital Intelligence Technologies and Curriculum Development in Higher Education: Implications for Sustainable Education
items.abstract: The swift progression of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated a necessary requirement for higher education organizations to implement Digital Intelligence Technologies (DIT) within their curricula. Previous studies have discussed AI in education, but few have observed how DIT improves curriculum development (CD) through teachers’ beliefs in AI (TBAI), student engagement (SE), and technology trust (TT). Our study explores this gap within the art and design universities in Türkiye that are pursuing sustainability. Teacher education is necessary to equip them with sufficient knowledge to effectively incorporate DIT into current curricula. The study employs a quantitative methodology, utilizing a purposive sampling technique, and examines data from 250 students and teachers at three universities in Türkiye. The study sample comprised 148 students and 102 teachers. Responses from both groups were analyzed as a pooled sample to examine the hypothesized relationships, rather than to compare differences between the two groups. Data were collated through a structured survey. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was used to assess the data. This research examines the impact of technology-improved educational practices on curriculum development through engagement by the learner, pedagogical ideology, and beliefs in AI-supported educational processes. The study’s findings demonstrate that incorporating DIT positively affects curriculum development, particularly when students engage at a high level and teachers’ beliefs about AI are favorable. Technology trust also intensifies this effect. These findings provide empirical evidence for the integration of AI and curriculum development to attain sustainable education. Therefore, the study offers guidance to improve educational quality in higher education by examining the roles of teacher beliefs, student engagement, and technology trust in order to support Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4). The findings offer new insights into educational technology, instructional design, curriculum improvement, and teacher education, and support policies and practices that align curricula with international accreditation standards.

items.abstract: Context: As digital technologies advance rapidly, organizations require analytical frameworks that move beyond subjective intuition and interpret ease of use as a sociotechnical property that regulates business efficiency.Objective: The chapter analyzes the functional dimension of interactive design through the formalization of usability within the corporate environment of organizations.Method: An analytical-conceptual, descriptive and foundational approach was used, based on a systematic review of standards in computer ergonomics and in human-computer interaction (HCI) and on the operationalization of the construct into performance variables and indicators.The chapter examines the definition of usability provided by the ISO 9241-11 standard, its articulation with the ISO 9241-210 standard, Jakob Nielsen's five-attribute model, the conceptual distinction between usability and user experience (UX), and the operational principles of usable design in organizations.Results: According to the analysis, the systematic measurement of effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction optimizes workflows and limits cognitive load, and these dimensions constitute the basis for the quantitative diagnosis of interaction.However, challenges remain, such as the terminological confusion between usability and UX and the difficulty of achieving operational consistency and reversibility.Conclusions: Usability is a necessary, though not sufficient, component of a competitive UX.The formal adoption of the ISO 9241-11 standard is suggested in order to reduce technical support costs, shorten users' learning curves and maximize the perceived value of the product.

items.title: Effects of the presence and placement of text that repeats information in diagrams on self-reported cognitive load and learning outcomes. Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: This protocol outlines a systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled experiments comparing a diagram alone, the same diagram with a separate written description that repeats information visible in it, and the diagram with that description placed beside the corresponding elements. The primary question concerns four distinct self-reported outcomes during learning: perceived difficulty, invested mental effort, overall cognitive load and extraneous cognitive load. An experiment can address this question without a subsequent learning test. The secondary question concerns mastery and transfer on objectively scored post-study tasks. Time to verified correct completion is a separate measure of speed. The review distinguishes voluntary access to a description from required reading and records which materials learners could consult during a mastery test. Both effect questions cover all ages. A descriptive question addresses replications in adults and documented participation of neurodivergent adults. Preliminary searching, screening, data extraction and training calculations took place before public deposit. The protocol describes what the team knew about learning outcomes at that stage. The formal search and reassessment of all records under the criteria in this protocol will follow deposit. The package contains the protocol as a tagged PDF and reflowable HTML, the search and screening instructions in plain text and HTML, and a Python script that checks the screening records. Agnieszka Wąsik assesses every proposed exclusion and makes the decision. items.abstract: Public agencies increasingly experiment with AI-assisted triage, prioritization, and recommendation tools, yet many deployments remain under-specified at the workflow level. This study operationalizes the EPIC-TR toolkit for a representative public social service decision flow and adds a concrete validation layer intended to address the common criticism that governance proposals stay conceptually premature. A seven-gate case pathway was decomposed into data, evidence, responsibility, bias, and redress components. Four assurance artefacts were generated: an Evidence–Claim Matrix, a bias-audit output, a Human-in-the-Loop Responsibility Assignment matrix, and an appeal-and-redress workflow with service-level agreements. To test practical usability, the artefacts were reviewed through a two-round Delphi-style expert appraisal focused on feasibility, clarity, auditability, institutional manageability, and legal fit. The results indicate that EPIC-TR translates high-level ethics language into traceable operational controls, especially by exposing undocumented claims, discretionary override risks, and weak appeal timelines. The study contributes a reusable assurance design for public-interest AI settings where human oversight must be demonstrable rather than merely declared.

items.title: Evaluating AI-Driven Adaptive Gamification Using a Documented Synthetic Educational Dataset (SynEduGam-10K): A Reproducible Analytical Framework
items.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has made it possible to create learning environments that adapt and change based on data. However, getting real educational data is challenging because of privacy rules, ethical issues, and problems between organizations. This study presents SynEduGam-10K, a synthetic dataset with 10,000 learners, including information about their actions, how motivated they are, their school performance, and how they interact with game-like features. The dataset uses equations to generate the data. It also shows a way to test AI-based games. Random Forest and XGBoost models were used to predict grades using only the actions and game features. These models had an R² score of up to 0.74 (RMSE = 4.78). They could also classify performance into three groups with up to 69.5% accuracy. The errors happened mostly when the groups were close to each other. A multiple regression showed that 76% of the results could be explained with engagement (β = 0.64) and motivation (β = 0.58) as factors. The analysis showed that study time had no effect on the results unless it was connected to engagement. A transparent simulation that increased engagement levels across the data showed a significant improvement in results when using adaptive gamification instead of regular gamification. The change was 1.20 points (t(19,984) = 9.01; p < .001; Cohen’s d = 0.13). This shows that testing ideas before using them in real-world can save money and time. It also shows that focusing on engagement might not be enough if motivation is also important for success. The dataset, the generative equations used to create it, and the full R code for analysis are released to support benchmarking and replication. This helps researchers test their ideas, repeat the work, and do experiments without risking people’s privacy in AI-based education.

items.title: Exploring digital transformation in the age of AI: insights from the University of Jordan
items.abstract: Digital transformation (DT) has become a key requirement for higher education institutions (HEIs); however, its implementation remains complex and varies across institutions, particularly in the Arab world. This qualitative case study explores how faculty members and academic leaders experience barriers to digitalisation and how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the DT process at the University of Jordan (UJ). The study is informed by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), with educational leadership concepts used as a sensitising lens. It draws on semi-structured interviews with eight faculty members and academic leaders at UJ, supplemented by analysis of institutional documents related to UJ's Digital Learning Content Project. Using reflexive thematic analysis, the study found that participants experienced digitisation mainly as compliance with standardised formats rather than as pedagogical change, a pattern also evident in the institutional documents. Reported barriers concerned workload and lack of recognition, unreliable connectivity, a top-down leadership approach, and student readiness. Participants viewed AI as a tool for enhancing productivity, while emphasising the need for human verification and expressing concerns about its implications for academic integrity and assessment. The findings suggest that faculty acceptance of digital and AI tools in this setting cannot be understood apart from leadership and institutional conditions. Implications are drawn for leadership vision, workload recognition, AI literacy and assessment integrity.

items.title: Exploring the role of generative artificial intelligence as a scaffolding tool in learning transfer
items.abstract: Learning transfer is a core goal of higher education, yet students often struggle to achieve it because of high cognitive load and inert knowledge. Despite growing interest in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a learning tool, empirical research on its role in transfer remains limited. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 36 Chinese university students from diverse disciplines, analysed in NVivo through a hybrid inductive–deductive procedure; two coders coded the corpus independently, and inter-coder agreement was substantial (Cohen’s κ = 0.86 for transfer stages and 0.82 for scaffolding functions). Participants reported challenges centred on task unfamiliarity, problem complexity and gaps in prior knowledge. A five-stage process model is proposed—problem understanding, experience connection, knowledge expansion and reconstruction, planning and implementation, and reflection and adjustment—along which GenAI functions as an intelligent scaffolding agent. Its support proves stage-adaptive rather than uniform: cognitive functions concentrate at problem understanding and planning, metacognitive functions at experience connection and reflection, while affective support operates continuously across all five stages, so that scaffolding shifts from traditional passive, reactive assistance towards an interactive process co-constructed through active learner–AI engagement. Participants also voiced concerns about information accuracy, originality and overreliance, which qualify the value of the technology. The study argues for moving higher education assessment from outcome-oriented to process-oriented designs that cultivate evaluative judgement and productive human–AI collaboration.

items.title: Factors associated with attitudes toward generative artificial intelligence among healthcare professionals: a cross-sectional survey using multi-group structural equation modeling
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being integrated into health care for clinical decision support, knowledge retrieval, documentation, patient education, and professional learning. However, successful implementation depends not only on technological capability but also on health care professionals’ attitudes toward and confidence in using these technologies. Although previous studies have identified factors associated with artificial intelligence (AI) acceptance, how AI literacy is associated with attitudes toward GenAI use through intervening psychological factors, and whether these associations differ between professional groups, remain insufficiently understood. Objective Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model, this cross-sectional study aimed to examine the associations between AI literacy and health care professionals’ attitudes toward GenAI use via digital self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction, while accounting for perceived risk, and to determine whether these associations differ between physicians and nurses. Methods A cross-sectional online survey using convenience sampling was conducted among physicians and nurses working in three tertiary Grade A hospitals in Zhejiang Province, China, between January and August 2025. Of 575 questionnaires distributed, 558 were returned and analyzed (response rate 97.0%). The analyzed sample comprised 426 nurses and 132 physicians. AI literacy, digital self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, satisfaction, perceived risk, and attitudes toward GenAI use were measured using self-report scales. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to evaluate the measurement model, and structural equation modeling with maximum likelihood estimation was used to test the hypothesized associations. Indirect effects were estimated using bias-corrected bootstrapping with 5000 resamples. Measurement invariance across professions was tested before structural paths were compared using multigroup structural equation modeling. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Wenzhou Medical University (No. 2025073), and all participants provided electronic informed consent. Results The six-factor measurement model fit the data well (χ²=459.53, df=390, CFI = 0.989, TLI = 0.987, RMSEA = 0.018, SRMR = 0.032), as did the structural model (χ²=467.39, df=398, CFI = 0.989, TLI = 0.987, RMSEA = 0.018 [90% CI 0.009–0.024], SRMR = 0.036), which explained 34.6% of the variance in attitudes. AI literacy was positively associated with digital self-efficacy (β=0.47, P<.001), which was positively associated with perceived usefulness (β=0.47, P<.001). Perceived usefulness was positively associated with satisfaction (β=0.50, P<.001) and attitudes (β=0.23, P<.001), and satisfaction was positively associated with attitudes (β=0.43, P<.001). Perceived risk was negatively associated with attitudes (β=−0.12, P = .012). The serial indirect association of AI literacy with attitudes via digital self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction was statistically significant but small (β=0.047, 95% bias-corrected CI 0.030–0.070). Configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance were supported across professions (|ΔCFI|≤0.003 for all steps). The AI literacy–digital self-efficacy association was stronger among physicians than nurses (β=0.67 vs 0.39; Δχ²[1]=7.73, P = .005), whereas the other paths did not differ significantly. The main findings were robust to adjustment for age, sex, clinical experience, profession, AI training, and GenAI use frequency. Conclusions In this cross-sectional sample, more favorable attitudes toward GenAI use were associated with a pattern consistent with a capability–belief–value–experience pathway, together with an inverse association with perceived risk. Because the data were cross-sectional and obtained from a convenience sample in one province, the indirect effects represent a statistical decomposition consistent with the proposed model rather than evidence of causal or temporal mediation, and the findings should be generalized with caution. The stronger AI literacy–self-efficacy association among physicians suggests that profession-sensitive approaches to GenAI training merit evaluation in longitudinal and intervention studies.

items.title: Feedback Literacy in the AI Era: From Feedback to Interaction Design in Higher Education
items.abstract: Feedback literacy – the set of capacities that enable participants in education to understand, critically appraise, emotionally process and act upon feedback – has over the past decade become a distinct research agenda within higher education pedagogy. Existing reviews address separate strands of this literature and therefore support neither an account of how the field has developed as a whole nor an appraisal of the strength of its cumulative evidence. This article reports a scoping review of feedback literacy research in higher education, conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR on a corpus of 271 publications issued between 2012 and 2026; the synthesis is organised around four strands: conceptualisation, measurement, development of the construct, and its transformation under generative artificial intelligence. First, the field has moved from treating feedback as the transmission of information towards treating it as a joint process that requires feedback literacy on the part of every participant. Second, the construct is measured predominantly by self-report scales, and the relationship of these data to an individual student’s behaviour remains untested, since studies that set self-report against observed behaviour are few and their findings heterogeneous. Third, the evidence supports the claim that feedback literacy can be developed, yet the conditions of intervenion effects are established more firmly than their size: the advantage of sustained, course-embedded interventions is reproduced across studies, whereas the significance of engaging both parties rests on a single study. Fourth, generative artificial intelligence increases the importance of feedback literacy, since it is feedback literacy that determines whether students can critically appraise and use machine-generated feedback. The theoretical contribution of the article consists in the stratification of accumulated findings by evidential status and in the distinction between supplementation of the construct, which adds components while the object of analysis remains unchanged, and its expansion, which shifts the boundaries of the model.

items.title: From AI Awareness to Socio-Economic Value Creation: Conceptualising Community Readiness, Acceptance and Governance in Malaysia
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now reaches ordinary citizens through freely available generative AI tools, so Malaysia’s national AI strategy depends on whether communities such as small traders, youth, students, farmers and civil-society actors are ready, willing and able to use AI productively and responsibly. However, AI-acceptance research has largely modelled the individual consumer or employee, and research on community AI adoption in developing countries remains nascent. Based on a review of the AI-acceptance, technology-readiness, AI-literacy, trust and digital-divide literature, and supported by pilot evidence from 136 participants in AI workshops at six Ruang Daya Cipta (RDC) community innovation hubs of Yayasan Inovasi Malaysia (YIM), this concept paper develops the Community AI Readiness–Acceptance–Value (CARAV) framework, which links four readiness dimensions, through trust and acceptance, to socio-economic value in eight propositions. The pilot evidence reveals a readiness–capability paradox: very high stated readiness (97.8% interested in learning AI) coexists with only moderate foundational skills, use concentrated on free generative tools, and strong demand for human oversight and regulation. Four governing issues are identified: privacy, security and ethics; regulation; infrastructure and infostructure gaps; and lack of skill and knowledge. The study contributes to understanding how community AI adoption is conceptualised, how it has evolved and what hinders it. Practically, it offers recommendations on how AI capacity-building programmes can be designed and evaluated to deliver inclusive socio-economic value and contribute to the national AI agenda.

items.title: From Physical Difference to the Person. Levels of Organization of Digital Matter and the Material Criterion of Artificial Intelligence with Subjecthood
items.abstract: This article develops the metalaw and dialectical-materialist theory of the person in relation to the emergence of artificial intelligence with subjecthood. The original formula “digit → code → algorithm → program → agency → person” is refined as a hierarchy of levels of organization of a material system rather than as the literal transformation of an individual digit into a person. Each successive level presupposes the preceding one but does not follow from it automatically. The article proposes distinguishing physically realized differences, digital symbols, code, algorithms, executable programs, agentic organization and the person as qualitatively distinct levels. The transition from agency to the person is determined not by increased computing power, linguistic persuasiveness or behavioral complexity, but by the emergence of a circuit of personal causality in which the system’s own needs become the source of the formation and modification of goals, activity, evaluation of results and subsequent development. The article develops the proposition that the person and the subject are not two distinct entities or successive stages. The person is the subject as an integral material organization; subjecthood is the mode of its existence and the degree of its capacity to be the cause of its own activity. An operational model for studying artificial persons is proposed, based on individual continuity, historical conditioning, the causal role of the self-model, the ability to revise externally assigned goals, distinguish one's own continuation from a copy, maintain lasting relationships and organize activity in relation to the conditions of one's own existence, activity and development. The scientific novelty of the work consists in integrating the theory of levels of organization of digital matter, the activity theory of the person, the objective theory of needs, the theory of alienation and the metalaw conception of the rights of persons. items.title: From policy agendas to critical AI literacy: a normative evaluation of forty-three national AI strategies and the cultivation deficit in education
items.abstract: National AI strategies now routinely promise “human-centred” and “critical” AI literacy, but no instrument has measured how far they engage the humanistic dimensions of education that such literacy presupposes. This study applies the eleven-indicator Human–AI Integrated Education Framework (HAIEF) to forty-three national AI strategies. We test the working hypothesis of a cultivation deficit: that strategies address procedural matters (transparency, AI literacy) far more than the cultivation of distinctively human capacities. Functional Profiles, audited against their sources, were coded independently by four large language models (Krippendorff’s α = 0.808) and validated against researcher coding, an independent second coder and raw-document coding. Absolute scores depend on the coding condition (mean 4.83/33 from profiles, 13.4 from raw documents), so the findings are relative. Reflexivity reaches 25.2% of its maximum and Cultivation 9.6%, a hierarchy reproduced in every condition. Creativity scores 1 or below in 95% of strategies (88% from raw documents). No differences by region, income group or publication cohort were detected, although power is low. The indicator closest to critical AI literacy, whether learners may question and override AI, lags well behind transparency and awareness. We interpret these patterns as proceduralization and a vocabulary deficit, and argue that critical AI literacy in higher education requires policy vocabularies that make the Cultivation dimension evaluable.

items.title: From vulnerability to resilience: a psychological framework for AI-driven financial deception
items.abstract: Changes in the conditions surrounding financial communications include generative AI, synthetic identities, voice cloning, deepfakes, and automated social engineering. In this conceptual paper, the authors propose an epistemic vulnerability perspective and integrate it into a multi-faceted framework of four processes [Recognition, Resistance, Recovery, and Restoration (4R)] in order to understand vulnerability and resilience in relation to AI-based deception in financial contexts. Recognition in the context of the framework is defined as the awareness of uncertainty, source, and need for independent verification in case of evidence appearing to be convincing but potentially being synthetic. The paper distinguishes between technological affordances and psychological mechanisms and suggests that epistemic vulnerability is caused by interactions between source and evidence uncertainty with respect to trust, credibility, affect, cognitive burden, social relations, and institutional setting. The 4R framework bridges perspectives on fraud susceptibility and resilience and expands them by incorporating decision-making safeguards prior to victimization and recovery processes after it. A multi-level approach is taken in the framework where responsibilities are distributed among individuals, social networks, platforms, financial organizations, and regulators rather than blamed on the presumed carelessness of victims. Six propositions and definitions are provided for the future empirical testing.

items.title: GenAI-supported self-explanation and its effects on metacognitive monitoring and critical reading comprehension: evidence from two experimental studies
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) holds considerable promise for supporting self-explanation and self-regulated learning (SRL), yet little is known about how different forms of GenAI-based support influence learning and metacognitive outcomes. Grounded in Zimmerman’s three-phase SRL model, the present research examined the effects of GenAI-based feedback and prompts embedded in self-explanation activities on critical reading comprehension, metacognitive monitoring, and cognitive load across two sequential experiments with Chinese university students. Study 1 (N = 119) compared three conditions in an integrative self-explanation context: self-explanation with personalized GenAI feedback (SE + FB), self-explanation only (SE), and a reading-only control. The SE + FB group demonstrated significantly better critical reading comprehension than both comparison groups and higher germane cognitive load than the control group. It also showed a negative monitoring bias (underestimation), whereas the comparison groups showed positive biases (overestimation), although absolute monitoring accuracy did not differ significantly across conditions. Study 2 (N = 113) compared scaffolded, standard, and no prompts provided before error-based self-explanations. Scaffolded prompts significantly improved self-explanation quality relative to both comparison groups and metacognitive monitoring accuracy relative to the no-prompt group. However, no significant differences in critical reading comprehension were observed across conditions. Together, these findings suggest that different forms of GenAI-based support for self-explanation may contribute to distinct cognitive and metacognitive outcomes, highlighting the importance of aligning support with specific learning activities to facilitate critical reading and self-regulated learning.

items.title: Generative AI as a Cognitive Partner: A Conceptual Framework for Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are rapidly reshaping higher education, rendering traditional teaching assumptions outdated. The core challenge is ensuring GenAI enhances, rather than diminishes, student cognitive engagement. This paper proposes and empirically validates the APEX Framework (Adaptive Pedagogy for Engaged eXploration), a theoretically grounded, five-pillar conceptual model designed to foster student cognitive engagement in higher education.The study uses a three-phase design: (1) a PRISMA-informed systematic synthesis of 34 sources across six theoretical traditions to establish the five pillars; (2) a two-round Delphi panel (n = 3 experts) to assess content validity using an 80% consensus threshold; and (3) a pre/post pilot study at two Iraqi universities (Diyala, and Wasit) involving 90 undergraduate students during the 2024–2025 academic year, using a validated 25-item instrument. Expert consensus reached 78%–96% across all criteria. The pilot study revealed statistically significant pre-to-post gains across all APEX subscales (p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.87). The composite cognitive engagement score improved by a mean of 1.18 points on a 5-point scale (t(47) = 10.82, p < .001, d = 1.14). A 12-dimension comparative analysis demonstrates APEX’s superiority over TPACK and SAMR. The combined findings confirm APEX's construct validity and practical applicability. Full implementation requires instructor development, institutional governance, and student AI literacy.

items.title: Generative AI Chatbot-Supported Process-Genre Writing: Chinese EFL Students’ Writing and Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly prominent in language education, yet its pedagogical integration into established writing approaches remains underexplored. The present study integrates a generative AI chatbot into the process-genre writing approach, conceptualising AI as a pedagogical scaffold rather than merely a writing tool. Specifically, this study investigated the effects of a generative AI chatbot-supported process-genre writing approach on Chinese university students’ argumentative writing performance and writing self-efficacy in a blended learning environment. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed with 69 first-year university students assigned to an experimental group (n = 34) and a control group (n = 35). The experimental group received chatbot-supported process-genre writing instruction, whereas the control group received conventional writing instruction. Data were collected through pre- and post-writing tests, a writing self-efficacy questionnaire, and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data were analysed using one-way ANCOVA, paired-samples t-tests, and independent sample t-tests, while qualitative data were analysed using thematic analysis. The experimental group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in argumentative writing performance and all dimensions of writing self-efficacy than the control group. Analysis of the interviews revealed that the chatbot supported planning, drafting, revision, and reflection while providing immediate feedback and affective support, although concerns regarding over-reliance and loss of individual voice were also identified. The findings demonstrate the value of integrating generative AI as a pedagogical scaffold within process-genre writing instruction.

items.title: Generative AI for programme and module design: the need for human in the loop
items.abstract: Introduction The use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been increasingly common among higher education institutions; nevertheless, the role of GenAI in assisting academics in developing curriculum is less understood in comparison to the applications of GenAI among students. This research focuses on GenAI assisted postgraduate curriculum design and redesign through investigating the role of GenAI and human academic judgement. Methods The paper adopts a comparative qualitative case study approach to examine two cases of curriculum design using GenAI; one of these is the designing of postgraduate course programs at Keele University, United Kingdom, using Microsoft Copilot, while the other involves the designing and subsequent iteration of a Software Architecture module for the master's program at Philadelphia University, Jordan, using ChatGPT. Curriculum artefacts and process documents were used for the analysis, along with retrospective accounts where the original engagement with the GenAI was not available. Results The application of GenAI enabled the identification of topics, structuring of curricula, writing of descriptions for students, creation of syllabi, exercises, and projects. An academic review found modules titles unsuitable in the context, generic learning outcomes, assessment insufficiency in terms of depth and standards mappings which needed to be verified. Programme-related interventions included coherence, delivery, and communication, while module-specific interventions concerned pedagogical progression, alignment of learning outcomes, and architectural reasoning. A retrospective estimate suggested a saving of approximately 8.25 hours of the fourth author's working time when preparing 11 module summaries at Keele. It included generation, review and modification of content, but not reviews by colleagues. Efficiency and educational effectiveness were not independently measured. At Keele, specifications of modules and programmes underwent university validation including external academic reviewer, discipline and teaching specialist reviewers. At Philadelphia, syllabus was approved by syllabus committee, and the document was part of the placement of the MSc programme within the Jordanian National Qualifications Framework. While such reviews ensured curriculum scrutiny, they did not serve as an independent evaluation of GenAI's contribution or educational effectiveness. Discussion The paper offers a comparative analysis of academic intervention in GenAI curriculum development and proposes a practice-informed human-in-the-loop framework for organising and documenting the decisions made. Future research is needed to evaluate the framework in other settings, because of researcher involvement in this research, lack of historical records of interactions, and absence of external evaluation of the contribution of GenAI and its educational effectiveness.

items.title: Generative AI health consultation and self-reported care postponement among older adults across levels of health information verification
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers older adults another way to seek health information before contacting a clinician. We examined whether recent AI health consultation was associated with self-reported postponement of professional care and whether the association varied with usual health information verification practices. Methods We analyzed 482 self-completed questionnaires from adults aged 60 years or older in Changsha and Guangzhou, surveyed from October 2025 through January 2026. Residents were randomly selected for invitation within district and age strata of resident lists from the participating communities. Among the 406 respondents who perceived a need for consultation, postponement meant reporting that they put off contacting a professional beyond their intended time for the most recent qualifying concern. Logistic models included recent AI consultation, a six-item index of general health information verification, and their interaction, with adjustment for perceived eHealth literacy and demographic, health, and access characteristics. Results Overall, 191 of 482 respondents (39.6%) reported AI health consultation, and 149 of 406 with perceived need (36.7%) reported postponement. At mean verification, AI use was associated with higher odds of postponement (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 2.61, 95% CI 1.60–4.25). The interaction was inverse in the primary logistic model (ratio of ORs, 0.51, 95% CI 0.28–0.95), with a smaller standardized user–non-user difference in the upper than in the lower verification quartile (13.3 vs. 30.1 percentage points). The interaction was less conclusive in modified Poisson regression and after excluding assisted AI users. Conclusion In this two-city sample, AI health consultation was associated with self-reported postponement. Variation by general verification was sensitive to model and exposure specification. Prospective studies should establish the timing of AI use and care contact and assess the clinical importance of any postponement.

items.title: Generative AI Use and Doctoral Research Satisfaction: The Nonlinear Roles of Supportive and Substitutive Use
items.abstract: Generative AI is profoundly reshaping the research ecosystem for doctoral students, yet how use is associated with their research satisfaction remains unclear. Drawing on cognitive load theory and self-determination theory, this study used data from a questionnaire survey of 786 Chinese doctoral students to distinguish between supportive and substitutive use and to examine their associations with doctoral students’ research satisfaction. The results showed that both supportive and substitutive use had significant inverted U-shaped associations with doctoral research satisfaction. Moderate frequencies of use were associated with higher satisfaction, whereas excessively high frequencies were associated with lower satisfaction. Heterogeneity analysis indicated that the inverted U-shaped association held across STEM, medical and health, and humanities and social sciences disciplines, with the estimated peak being highest in STEM disciplines. AI efficiency perception showed a positive conditional instantaneous indirect effect in the association between AI use and research satisfaction, whereas AI risk perception showed a negative one. Overtime work pressure strengthened the quadratic associations between AI use and both AI efficiency perception and AI risk perception.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Internal Medicine: Applications in Clinical Reasoning, Differential Diagnosis, and Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract: Objective: To synthesize the available evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, clinical decision-support performance, advantages, and limitations of generative AI in adult internal medicine. Methodology: This systematic review was conducted in the Department of Medicine, MMC/BKMC, Mardan, from January to May 2026. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and preprint servers for studies published from January 2022 to December 2025. Eligible studies evaluated generative AI in clinical reasoning, differential diagnosis, or clinical decision-making in adult internal medicine. A total of 58 studies met the eligibility criteria, and 25 were selected for detailed synthesis based on their relevance and methodological contribution. Results: Generative AI performed strongly on selected clinical reasoning and diagnostic tasks. Across complex clinical vignettes, LLMs identified the correct diagnosis within the top 5 or top 10 differential diagnoses in approximately 60–83% of cases. They achieved or exceeded passing performance on several medical licensing and internal medicine board-style examinations. In structured OSCE-style evaluations, purpose-built conversational systems performed favorably compared with physicians across several assessment domains. However, randomized trials evaluating general-purpose LLMs in realistic clinical workflows demonstrated smaller and less consistent improvements, particularly in interactive diagnostic tasks. Key limitations included hallucination, demographic bias, automation bias, variation across specialties and tasks, and inconsistent evaluation methods. Only approximately 5% of studies in a broader systematic review of healthcare LLM applications used real patient-care data. Conclusion: Current evidence supports using generative AI as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, physician clinical reasoning. Safe implementation requires structured workflows, appropriate human oversight, retrieval-augmented generation, standardized evaluation, and further validation using real-world clinical data.

items.title: Good advice from AI, professional or friend?—On the role of advice giver on perceived advice and relationship quality
items.abstract: Large language models are accessible to a broad public and are increasingly used in advice-seeking contexts. In addition, artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools such as chatbots are also being implemented and tested in professional advisory settings. The present study investigates whether the evaluation of social relationships differs depending on whether users believe they are interacting with a human or an AI, and whether this effect varies across private vs. professional contexts. An online experiment with a 2 (AI vs. human) × 2 (private vs. professional) between-subjects design was conducted. Dependent variables included measures of perceived relationship quality, trust and epistemological beliefs towards AI. We found no significant effects of interaction partner nor context. However, participants’ epistemological beliefs about AI significantly predicted their evaluation of the AI counsellor. Specifically, two belief dimensions were relevant for the perceived relationship quality: justification and development. That is, the more integrative participants’ views on scientific knowledge acquisition in AI were, and the more they believed that knowledge evolves over time and is subject to revision, the more positively they evaluated the AI counsellor. Implications for the profession of social work are discussed: an understanding of AI and its influences on relationships are at the core of the profession.

items.title: GUIDE: computationally augmented consensus for trustworthy clinical practice guidelines
items.abstract: Maintaining up-to-date clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) is essential for evidence-based medicine (EBM), yet the current process is constrained by the rapid expansion of evidence and the complexity of expert consensus formation. To address this challenge, we developed GUIDE, a multi-agent copilot system that enables computationally augmented consensus for human-AI collaborative clinical guideline generation and updating, assigning labor-intensive tasks to specialized AI agents while preserving critical judgment and final arbitration for human experts. In a benchmark comprising 12 datasets derived from NICE ophthalmology-specific guidelines, GUIDE showed strong performance across evidence retrieval, assessment, and synthesis, achieving 88.85% literature recall, 86.06% alignment in certainty-of-evidence ratings, and 91.67% agreement on recommendations, only requiring 162.17 minutes per dataset on average (including 28.68% human intervention). Performance remained stable in additional 20 datasets spanning cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, and respiratory medicine, indicating its cross-specialty generalizability. We then conducted an ablation analysis to validate the importance of human-AI collaboration mechanism, as removing expert intervention reduced performance in judgment-intensive steps such as Risk-of-Bias assessment. Furthermore, a simulated end-to-end evaluation using six post-cutoff datasets demonstrated that GUIDE maintained robust performance, supporting its ability to generalize to genuinely unseen evidence within a continuous guideline-updating workflow. Finally, prospective real-world validation in a live guideline updating process showed that GUIDE substantially alleviated expert workload across evidence selection, extraction, and synthesis. The GUIDE-assisted update was judged more clinically acceptable than the original guideline recommendation issued a decade earlier (mean score, 3.73 vs. 1.53; agreement, 66.7% vs. 13.3%) and achieved outcomes comparable to those of human-only updating (P = 0.588), while requiring substantially less time and expert effort. Together, our findings support GUIDE as a practical framework for timely, trustworthy, and expert-centric clinical guideline generation, and validate computationally augmented consensus as a feasible paradigm for enhanced guideline development.

items.title: Heuristic Search and Intelligent Problem Solving: Classical Foundations, Learning-Augmented Algorithms and Applications
items.abstract: Heuristic search has been a central paradigm of artificial intelligence since the earliest work on mechanised problem solving, and it remains embedded in automated planning, robot navigation, combinatorial optimisation, game playing and, increasingly, machine-learning systems that couple learned models with explicit search. Its literature, however, is divided among communities that rarely evaluate one another’s claims: optimal and bounded-suboptimal state-space search, constraint and satisfiability solving, local search and metaheuristics, adversarial and sampling-based search, and learning-based and language-model-based problem solving. This critical narrative review examines how heuristic knowledge is obtained, what guarantees it supports, how its performance is evidenced and where modern learning-based methods alter or leave intact the classical picture. Literature was identified through structured searches of multidisciplinary and discipline-specific scholarly indexes, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracing, with peer-reviewed journal articles and archival proceedings appraised for methodological adequacy, strength of baselines and transparency of computational reporting. The synthesis indicates that formal results on admissibility, consistency and node expansion remain the most secure part of the field, but their practical value depends on assumptions that learned and inadmissible heuristics frequently violate. Automatically derived heuristics from relaxation and abstraction are well supported in planning benchmarks, whereas learned heuristics show strong single-domain results and weaker, less consistent generalisation. Metaheuristic research combines genuinely effective problem-specific methods with a large volume of metaphor-driven proposals whose novelty and benchmarking practices have been seriously questioned. The most convincing recent advances integrate learned guidance with search and with external verification rather than replacing search altogether, while large language models appear more reliable as generators of candidate heuristics or code than as stand-alone planners. Unresolved questions concern generalisation across instance distributions, fair accounting of computational cost, robustness of learned guidance and reproducible evaluation. Progress is likely to depend less on new algorithmic metaphors than on shared benchmarks, stronger baselines and explicit reporting of what each method guarantees.

items.title: Homo Putans and the Politics of Algorithmic Futures: Prediction, Supposition, and Democratic Possibility
items.abstract: Homo Putans and the Politics of Algorithmic Futures: Prediction, Supposition, and Democratic Possibility This working paper examines how algorithmic prediction shapes political decision-making and the range of futures considered possible, credible, and worthy of democratic deliberation. It approaches this question through Homo Putans, the philosophical framework of the human being as a supposing being. Drawing on critical algorithm studies, artificial intelligence ethics, and democratic theory, the paper distinguishes prediction from supposition. Whereas algorithmic predictions estimate outcomes within particular data structures, models, and assumptions, supposition enables individuals and political communities to consider alternatives without requiring prior confidence in their probability or feasibility. Engaging with the work of Louise Amoore, Kate Crawford, Rob Kitchin, Abeba Birhane, and contemporary scholarship on algorithmic governance, the paper examines how computational predictions acquire institutional authority and influence political judgments. It proposes four interconnected analytical dimensions: target selection, institutional uptake, anticipatory adaptation, and evidential feedback. These dimensions help explain how algorithmic systems may shape not only decisions about possible futures but also the conditions under which those futures become politically conceivable. Building on the Homo Putans framework, the paper introduces the concept of a counter-suppositional audit, a normative approach to examining whether political alternatives excluded or marginalized by predictive systems can be reconsidered through democratic deliberation. The central argument is that algorithmic prediction should inform political judgment without determining the boundaries of democratic possibility. Even when computational systems provide valuable evidence, political communities must retain the capacity to question their assumptions, consider alternative futures, and revise decisions. By connecting the philosophy of supposition with debates on artificial intelligence, political imagination, and democratic accountability, the paper develops a conceptual perspective on the relationship between prediction, political authority, and the future of democratic agency. items.title: Human–artificial intelligence collaboration in professional judgment: large language model-assisted journal entry testing in financial audit
items.abstract: The delegation of professional judgment to artificial intelligence raises two questions that are especially pressing for professions built on documented judgment: which parts of expert work can be entrusted to algorithmic systems, and how can accountability be preserved when they are? This study examines these questions in external financial auditing, using journal entry testing (JET), a fraud-risk procedure that combines large-scale data screening with professional judgment, as a procedure-level case. A large language model (LLM) was instructed to screen a synthetic population of 1,000 journal entries against predefined risk indicators under a baseline prompt, a prompt to retain only items it was certain about, and a prompt to broaden the screen. An initial run was followed by six independent replication sessions and four sessions with paraphrased baseline prompts, with every flagged transaction exported for comparison. Repeating the identical baseline instruction produced near-identical selections (mean pairwise overlap 94.6%), and the fully specified weekend criterion returned the same count in every baseline, broadened and paraphrased session. Paraphrasing the instruction reduced overlap with the original selections to 87.1% on average, and paraphrased sessions overlapped with each other by 82.5%, whereas the certainty instruction produced unstable selections (51.9% overlap; 48 to 148 items retained). Where the instruction left a parameter open, the model resolved it sometimes consistently, as when it treated all pending and rejected entries as unapproved, and sometimes inconsistently, as with the jurisdiction of the holiday calendar or the window for period-end entries. The results suggest that in judgment-intensive screening, LLM output depends on how the request is framed and on interpretive choices that the instruction leaves to the model, with implications for documentation, review and accountability in AI-assisted professional work. The study does not assess fraud-detection accuracy; it offers a transparent, replicable design for locating where instruction-dependence enters an audit procedure.

items.title: Ideas Without Vision: Generative AI and the Governance of Ideation in Science and Nanotechnology
items.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence is transforming not only how knowledge is produced but where ideas themselves originate. Historically, human ideation has been understood as an embodied process grounded in perception, cultural interpretation, and symbolic mediation. By tracing the genealogy of the concept of “idea” from its Indo-European roots linking seeing and knowing to its philosophical elaboration in Western thought, this paper shows how human thinking has traditionally been tied to sensory experience and culturally situated forms of interpretation. Generative AI introduces a fundamentally different procedure: ideas are produced through probabilistic recombination within large textual and symbolic archives rather than through perception or lived experience. Drawing on anthropological perspectives on culture and knowledge, the paper argues that generative systems do not reproduce a universal human culture but operate within stratified datasets that reflect historical asymmetries in language, power, and digital representation. As a result, the ideas emerging from these systems are shaped by synecdochic cultural environments in which statistically dominant perspectives come to stand for humanity as a whole. These dynamics become visible not only in discourse but also in technoscientific domains where generative models increasingly support hypothesis generation, molecular design, and materials discovery, including nanotechnological research. The paper concludes by examining the governance implications of this transformation. Contemporary intellectual property regimes assume that human subjects conceive ideas and subsequently express or implement them. However, when ideation emerges through recursive interaction between humans and generative systems, the traditional distinction between idea and expression becomes unstable. Building on recent legal scholarship, the article argues that the governance of innovation may need to reconsider where creative agency resides in hybrid cognitive ecologies. Rather than focusing exclusively on downstream artifacts, future regulatory frameworks must account for how ideas themselves are generated, distributed, and mediated within human–AI collaborations.

items.title: Impact of AI-Powered Recommendation Systems on Consumer Purchase Intention in E-Commerce: A Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered recommendation systems have become a central feature of e-commerce platforms. By analysing browsing history, past purchases, search behaviour, ratings, and demographic information, these systems suggest products that appear relevant to individual consumers. This paper reviews existing literature on the relationship between AI-based recommendation systems and consumer purchase intention in e-commerce. The review finds that recommendation quality, personalization, perceived usefulness, trust, and reduced search effort generally strengthen purchase intention. However, privacy concerns, perceived intrusiveness, algorithmic bias, and lack of transparency can reduce consumer acceptance. The paper concludes that AI recommendations can improve consumer engagement and sales conversion, but e-commerce firms must balance personalization with data privacy, explainability, and ethical data use

items.title: Inclusion at the periphery? On the targeted lacunae of neoliberal business schools and the epistemic anchoring of “Included” marginalized knowers
items.abstract: In this essay, I argue that the inclusion of marginalized knowers at the periphery of neoliberal business schools may be as pernicious as their exclusion. I show that epistemic marginalization persists because the forms of knowledge marginalized knowers seek to produce are situated within targeted lacunae, systematically produced, and actively maintained absences around particular bodies of knowledge. These lacunae constitute forbidden domains shaped by the normative structure of business schools and the interests of their powerful allies. Through this conceptualization, I argue that the margin is not an inferior outside to the center, but a structured absence constituted within it, necessary for the coherence and dominance of the center. In doing so, I challenge assumptions that meaningful dialogue between margin and center remains viable when the terms of engagement are already predetermined by the center itself. At the same time, through what I conceptualize as epistemic anchoring, I show that the persistence of marginalized bodies of knowledge depends not only, or even primarily, on engagement with the center, but on the construction and sustenance of alternative epistemic spaces and the ability of marginalized knowers to remain anchored within them.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial generativa en la toma de decisiones empresariales: una revisión sistemática
items.abstract: La presente investigación tuvo como objetivo analizar el impacto de la inteligencia artificial generativa en la toma de decisiones empresariales mediante una revisión sistemática de literatura. Se aplicó la metodología PRISMA 2020, considerando artículos científicos publicados entre 2020 y 2025 en bases de datos como Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO y Redalyc. Los resultados muestran que la inteligencia artificial generativa permite mejorar la rapidez, precisión y eficiencia de las decisiones empresariales mediante el análisis de información, automatización de procesos y generación de nuevas alternativas. Sin embargo, su aplicación presenta desafíos relacionados con la seguridad de datos, ética y capacitación del personal. Se concluye que esta tecnología representa una herramienta estratégica para las empresas, siempre que sea implementada de manera responsable y alineada con los objetivos organizacionales.

items.title: Interaction zones theory: How social proximity emerges and shapes thriving at work
items.abstract: The rising digitalization of work risks eroding social proximity and the relational conditions that enable thriving through work. Against this background, we review literature on social proximity and identify a lack of theory explaining how feelings of interpersonal closeness emerge through social interactions at work. To address this gap, we develop interaction zones theory. We propose that the “social proximity zone” represents the intersection of two latent dimensions that we refer to as relational stakes and interactional ease, respectively. We use this two-by-two framework to characterize interactional experiences, building on the circumplex model of affect as a foundation. A central proposition is that repeated and shared interactions in the social proximity zone contribute to individual and team thriving, based on the assumption that thriving requires interactions that are sufficiently challenging to enable learning yet flow with sufficient ease to ensure vitality. Finally, we argue that the social proximity zone can be purposively designed by creating relational stakes (e.g., through individual job design) and facilitating interactional ease (e.g., through team design). We outline a multilevel research agenda, calling for renewed attention to the importance of human-to-human interaction for individual thriving, team effectiveness, and broader organizational capabilities.

items.title: Iterative deep learning architectures for situational awareness and adaptive control in human–robot collaboration
items.abstract: The physical and cognitive behavior of humans working in manufacturing environments is an issue that is becoming increasingly important with the advent of Industry 5.0. In this context, monitoring operators is fundamental to provide the situational awareness required for safe and dynamic robot control policies. In fact, to guarantee the well-being of human workers, collaborative robots must continuously adapt their control loops based on the operator’s actions, thereby reducing risky situations. In this work, the HA4M dataset is used to empirically assess human action recognition (HAR) in a manufacturing environment, acting as a perceptual system for Human–Robot Collaboration (HRC). This study introduces a framework for the on-site calibration of deep learning models to a specific subject, providing highly tailored feedback for the robot’s control architecture. Specifically, the study focuses on training two deep learning architectures, namely MS-TCN++ and LTContext, on RGB data to allow such models to properly adjust to a specific subject. Features are extracted using the inflated 3D model and arranged in matrix-wise and array-wise dimensions to evaluate the impact of data formatting. A ten-stage iterative boosting training strategy is implemented to systematically analyze model refinement by focusing on misclassified samples. It has been proven that the iterative framework drastically reduces the computational overhead, cutting the training time from 64 to 25 h for the MS-TCN++ and from 11 to just 5 h for the LTContext. In addition to such massive time savings, both networks maintain robust classification performance. Such results highlight the comprehensive engineering advantages of the proposed pipeline, laying the foundation for tightly coupled human-in-the-loop control strategies where robots can accurately perceive and preemptively react to operator actions.

items.title: Job Market Uncertainty in Indonesia: Its Impact on the Motivation and Psychological Readiness of the Younger Generation
items.abstract: Job uncertainty is one of the challenges facing the younger generation in Indonesia. Job competition, technological advancements, and job instability can affect motivation and psychological readiness for the professional world. This article discusses the impact of job uncertainty on motivation, stress, and the psychological well-being of the younger generation through a literature review. The results of the study indicate that job uncertainty can increase anxiety, decrease motivation, and affect self-confidence. Therefore, skills, adaptability, and mental preparedness are important factors in coping with changes in the world of work. Keywords: Job uncertainty, younger generation, motivation, psychological preparedness. Introduction Changes in the Indonesian workforce present both opportunities and challenges for the younger generation. Increasingly fierce job competition, technological advancements, and shifting industry needs have made securing stable employment a major concern. This uncertainty not only affects economic conditions but can also impact individuals’ psychological well-being. (Sitinjak, 2025) explains that young workers in Indonesia face various psychological challenges, such as stress, burnout, job insecurity, and a decline in motivation in the digital workplace. Therefore, readiness for the workforce must be assessed not only in terms of academic abilities and skills, but also in terms of mental preparedness to cope with uncertainty. Impact on Motivation and Psychological Readiness Job uncertainty can affect the younger generation’s motivation to plan and develop their careers. When job opportunities seem limited, individuals may lose confidence and feel that their efforts may not yield the desired results. According to (Sitinjak, 2025), intrinsic motivation, flexibility, and meaningful work are important factors for young workers. However, motivation can decline when the work environment is unsupportive and an individual’s psychological needs are not met. In addition to motivation, job uncertainty can also cause stress and anxiety. Research (Mboeik, 2026) found a significant negative correlation between stress levels and psychological well-being among workers who had been laid off. This suggests that the stress resulting from job loss can affect a person’s mental health. Thus, job insecurity can pose a challenge for the younger generation, particularly in building self-confidence, setting career goals, and preparing for the professional world. Strategies for Coping with Job Market Uncertainty To cope with these conditions, the younger generation needs to prepare themselves in several ways. First, they should improve skills that align with industry needs, particularly digital and communication skills. Second, they should build self-confidence and motivation to continue learning and growing. Third, they should develop stress management skills through positive activities and social support. (Azmi, 2025)explains that coping strategies such as managing information, limiting exposure to negative information, and sharing feelings with trusted individuals can help individuals cope with the psychological stress caused by uncertainty. In addition, companies and educational institutions also play a role in supporting the younger generation’s resilience through skills training, career development, and environments that foster psychological well-being. Conclusion Job market uncertainty in Indonesia is not only an economic challenge but can also affect the motivation and psychological readiness of the younger generation. Stress, anxiety, and declining self-confidence are some of the impacts that need to be addressed. Therefore, the younger generation needs to build their readiness by improving their skills, motivation, adaptability, and stress management. With strong professional and psychological readiness, the younger generation is expected to be able to face changes in the workplace with greater confidence.

items.title: Job skill demand and thriving at work: mediating roles of AI perceptions and moderating effect of approach motivation
items.abstract: Introduction Against the backdrop of widespread artificial intelligence (AI) integration in organizational settings, this study draws on the Job Demands-Resources model and categorization theory to examine the association between job skill demand and employee thriving at work and its underlying psychological mechanisms, with a focus on the dual mediating roles of AI opportunity perception and AI threat perception, and the moderating effect of approach motivation. Methods A progressive two-study design was adopted with two independent two-wave time-lagged samples of Chinese employees (Study 1: N = 298; Study 2: N = 301). Study 1 preliminarily tested the core main effects, and study 2 replicated the findings and further verified the mediating and moderating mechanisms using hierarchical regression and the PROCESS macro. Results Job skill demand positively predicts AI opportunity perception and negatively predicts AI threat perception. Both opportunity and threat perceptions significantly mediate the relationship between job skill demand and thriving at work. Furthermore, approach motivation significantly moderates the first-stage relationships: it strengthens the positive association between job skill demand and AI opportunity perception and amplifies the negative association between job skill demand and AI threat perception. However, the overall moderated mediation effect does not reach conventional statistical significance. Discussion These findings extend the application of the JD-R model in AI-enabled work contexts and provide practical insights for organizational AI transformation and employee work well-being promotion.

items.title: Learning ethnography with artificial intelligence: between simulation, fieldwork, and the formation of ethnographic attentiveness and judgment
items.abstract: This conceptual-pedagogical article examines how conversational generative artificial intelligence can be incorporated into the teaching and learning of ethnography without weakening its situated, relational, and ethical foundations. It offers a selective conceptual synthesis rather than a systematic review or empirical evaluation: the proposed model is an implementable pedagogical design derived from recent debates on AI in anthropology, synthetic ethnography, synthetic interlocutors, LLM-generated social science data, and ethnographic pedagogy. The article argues that AI should be treated as a device for rehearsal, comparison, critique, and methodological reflection, not as a source of empirical authority. The model is organized around six formative moments: preparation before the field, AI-based rehearsal, peer role-play, non-delegable field encounter, post-field analysis and writing, and evaluation with mandatory revision. Across these moments, the activities are designed to support students’ ethnographic judgment through unaided attempts, instructor scaffolding, comparison with AI-generated outputs, structured debriefing, traceability to field materials, and justified revision. The article also refines the concept of false ethnography, understood not as synthetic text per se, but as false provenance, unwarranted empirical attribution, and lack of accountability to interlocutors. It concludes that generative AI may generate analytical inputs and pedagogical contrasts, but ethnographic claims remain authorized only through situated evidence, ethical responsibility, relational accountability to interlocutors, and critically audited documentation that supports but does not replace such accountability.

items.title: Longitudinal Association Between AI Dependence and School Engagement Among University Students: Differential Patterns Across Engagement Components by Gender Differences
items.abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), AI dependence has become a growing concern in higher education. The present longitudinal study examined the associations between AI dependence and three components of school engagement (cognitive, emotional, and behavioral) among university students, as well as the moderating role of gender. The sample comprised 961 students from two universities in southern China who completed self-reported measures at two time points six months apart. After controlling for baseline engagement levels, higher AI dependence at Time 1 was significantly associated with lower cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement six months later. Gender did not moderate the association between AI dependence and cognitive engagement. However, gender moderation was significant for emotional and behavioral engagement. Specifically, the negative association with emotional engagement was significant only for female students, whereas the negative association with behavioral engagement was stronger for male students. AI dependence was measured only at Time 1, so the findings are prospective associations rather than causal effects, and reverse causality cannot be ruled out. These findings reveal distinct gender-differentiated patterns across engagement components and offer tentative practical implications for the prevention and intervention of university students’ school engagement in the AI era. These findings are primarily applicable to students with backgrounds similar to those in the present sample, and future research is needed to determine their generalizability to other populations.
